text: Norse religion was the old faith of Scandinavia, in the north of Europe, from about 1,500 years ago.
It grew from the older faith of the Germanic peoples and had no single founder.
src: Norse religion, the pre-Christian faith of Scandinavia / years: 500 to 1100 / region: Europe
from the religion of the Germanic peoples of the Iron Age / without a founder

text: Its followers worshipped many gods, such as Odin, the god of wisdom, poetry and magic.
In their stories Thor, the god of thunder, used his hammer to guard gods and humans against the giants.
src: worshipped gods such as Odin, Thor, Freyr and Freyja / Odin, chief of the Æsir, was the god of wisdom, poetry, magic, war and the dead
Thor, armed with his hammer Mjöllnir, was the god of thunder and the protector of gods and humans against the giants

text: In their myths, a great ash tree called Yggdrasil linked nine worlds, of gods, humans, giants and the dead.
Most of these myths were written down by Christians in Iceland, more than 700 years ago.
src: The cosmos was held together by the ash tree Yggdrasil, whose roots and branches linked nine worlds, among them Asgard of the gods, Midgard of humans, Jotunheim of the giants and Hel of the dead
known mainly from Icelandic texts written down by Christians in the 13th century

text: There were no priests or churches: chieftains, kings and the heads of families led the worship.
Some of the dead were buried with tools, animals and even ships, like the Oseberg ship in Norway.
src: Norse religion had no separate priesthood or church. / Religious rituals were led by the heads of households, by chieftains and by kings
The dead were cremated or buried with weapons, tools, animals and even ships, as in the magnificent ship burials of Oseberg, of 834, and Gokstad in Norway

text: Later, kings such as Olaf Tryggvason of Norway made their people become Christians, often by force.
More than 800 years ago, all of Scandinavia had become Christian.
src: In Norway, the kings Olaf Tryggvason, at the end of the 10th century, and Olaf Haraldsson, killed at the battle of Stiklestad in 1030 and soon venerated as a saint, imposed Christianity, often by force
By the 12th century Christianity had prevailed throughout Scandinavia

text: English still names Wednesday after Woden, or Odin, and Thursday after Thor.
Its myths still inspire music, books and films, like the operas of Richard Wagner.
src: Wednesday after Woden, the Norse Odin, Thursday after Thor

Richard Wagner drew on the Eddas and related sagas for his opera cycle The Ring of the Nibelung / comics, novels, films, television and video games have made Odin, Thor and Loki familiar around the world
